evidence.claim: Follow the Payette
evidence.quote: goes east on Highway 52 along the Payette River

evidence.claim: past a ferry town
evidence.quote: Emmett is a town on the southern bank of the Payette River that grew up around a ferry crossing of the Payette River.

evidence.claim: a fruit-growing valley
evidence.quote: the major service center for a farming and fruit-growing valley.

evidence.claim: The Lower Payette River Heritage Byway follows Highway 52 east from the Snake River through Payette, Emmett and Horseshoe Bend.
evidence.quote: Begins on the banks of the Snake River and goes east on Highway 52 along the Payette River, passing through the communities of Payette, Emmett and Horseshoe Bend.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho presents this scenic byway as a drive through rural scenery, with historic museums, parks and orchards among its attractions.
evidence.quote: the Lower Payette River Heritage Byway is 57 miles of rural views on Highway 52.

evidence.claim: with historic museums, parks and orchards among its attractions
evidence.quote: stop off for local cuisine, ziplining, historical museums, picturesque parks and more.

evidence.claim: orchards
evidence.quote: Fruit picking at local orchards

evidence.claim: The road is a paved, two-lane highway with occasional passing lanes, continuing into Black Canyon beyond Emmett.
evidence.quote: Highway 52 is a two lane paved secondary highway with occasional passing lanes.

evidence.claim: continuing into Black Canyon beyond Emmett
evidence.quote: then continuing east up Black Canyon to its terminus at Horseshoe Bend.

evidence.claim: Bluffs, the river and Black Canyon Reservoir give the journey its changing shape.
evidence.quote: Bluffs along Highway 52.

evidence.claim: the river and Black Canyon Reservoir
evidence.quote: All along the highway going east, the Black Canyon Dam and Reservoir provides a number of recreational sites.

evidence.claim: Speeds are restricted through the cities along the highway.
evidence.quote: Speed is restricted through the cities.

evidence.claim: The highway corridor existed by 1929 as part of State Highway 16. State Highway 52 was created in 1938, then extended west from Emmett toward New Plymouth, Payette and the state line in 1955.
evidence.quote: This route has been in existence since 1929, originally as part of State Highway 16

evidence.claim: State Highway 52 was created in 1938
evidence.quote: State Highway 52 was created in 1938

evidence.claim: then extended west from Emmett toward New Plymouth, Payette and the state line in 1955
evidence.quote: SH-16 was eventually truncated at Emmett in 1955, and SH-52 was then extended westward along the former SH-16 heading toward New Plymouth, and ending up in Payette and the state line.

evidence.claim: In the valley it crossed, irrigation projects had helped Emmett expand as a service center for farms and fruit growers.
evidence.quote: A series of irrigation projects made it possible for more rapid expansion of the town as the major service center for a farming and fruit-growing valley.

evidence.claim: Fruit packers adopted the name “Gem of Plenty” in the early 1900s, linking the valley’s identity to its crops.
evidence.quote: In the early 1900s fruit packers adopted the label of "Gem of Plenty" because of the fertility of the valley.

evidence.claim: Start at the Snake River and travel through Payette, whose beginnings lay in a railroad construction camp.
evidence.quote: The settlement was originally named "Boomerang," a construction camp for the Oregon Short Line from 1882 to 1884 at the mouth of the Payette River.

evidence.claim: Continue east to Emmett, then turn north with Highway 52 before following it east into Black Canyon.
evidence.quote: Then heads eastward to the city of Emmett where it turns north at its junction with SH-16 then continuing east up Black Canyon

evidence.claim: Beyond the dam and reservoir, Horseshoe Bend marks the highway’s end and the river’s horseshoe-shaped turn.
evidence.quote: It is named for its location at the horseshoe-shaped U-turn of the Payette River

evidence.claim: Horseshoe Bend marks the highway’s end
evidence.quote: to its terminus at Horseshoe Bend.

evidence.claim: Before it was Payette, the settlement was Boomerang, an Oregon Short Line construction camp at the river’s mouth from 1882 to 1884.
evidence.quote: The settlement was originally named "Boomerang," a construction camp for the Oregon Short Line from 1882 to 1884 at the mouth of the Payette River.

evidence.claim: The camp’s work depended on both water and rail: logs floated down the Payette to its sawmills, where they were sawn into ties for the new railroad.
evidence.quote: Logs were floated down the river to the sawmills at the camp to produce railroad ties.

evidence.claim: Once the railroad was finished, the settlement moved upstream to its present location.
evidence.quote: Logs were floated down the river to the sawmills at the camp to produce railroad ties. After completion of the railroad, the settlement moved upstream to its present site

evidence.claim: It incorporated as Payette in 1891, taking the name of French-Canadian fur trapper François Payette. He had headed the Hudson’s Bay Company’s Fort Boise trading post from 1835 to 1844.
evidence.quote: incorporated in 1891 as "Payette," to honor François Payette, a French-Canadian fur trapper

evidence.claim: He had headed the Hudson’s Bay Company’s Fort Boise trading post from 1835 to 1844.
evidence.quote: was later the head of the Fort Boise trading post for the British Hudson's Bay Company from 1835 to 1844.

evidence.claim: The town became the county seat when Payette County was created in 1917.
evidence.quote: Payette County was created in 1917, partitioned from Canyon County, and the city of Payette became the county seat.

evidence.claim: The “Gem of Plenty” label began with fruit packers in the early 1900s, when irrigation was helping Emmett grow into a service center for the surrounding farming valley.
evidence.quote: A series of irrigation projects made it possible for more rapid expansion of the town as the major service center for a farming and fruit-growing valley. In the early 1900s fruit packers adopted the label of "Gem of Plenty" because of the fertility of the valley.

evidence.claim: The town had developed beside a ferry built by Nathaniel Martin and Jonathan Smith. Its first name, Martinsville, gave way to Emmettville, a post-office name honoring an early settler’s son.
evidence.quote: Emmett was originally called Martinsville, named after Nathaniel Martin who, along with Jonathan Smith, built the ferry crossing.

evidence.claim: Emmettville, a post-office name honoring an early settler’s son
evidence.quote: Next, the name was changed to "Emmettville," because it was primarily a post office named after Emmett Cahalan, the son of Tom Cahalan, an early settler of the area.

evidence.claim: The post office moved, but the town kept the name, later shortened to Emmett. The Idaho Northern Railroad arrived in the valley in March 1902.
evidence.quote: The post office was later moved but the town retained the name. A few years later the "ville" was dropped and the post office and town became simply Emmett.

evidence.claim: The Idaho Northern Railroad arrived in the valley in March 1902.
evidence.quote: Later, in March 1902, the Idaho Northern Railroad came to the valley.

evidence.claim: East of the city stands Black Canyon Diversion Dam, originally completed in 1924 and reconstructed between 1951 and 1955.
evidence.quote: The concrete dam was originally completed in 1924, then re-constructed between 1951 and 1955

evidence.claim: East of the city stands Black Canyon Diversion Dam
evidence.quote: The Black Canyon diversion dam on the Payette River, built in the early 1920s, is east of the city.

evidence.claim: The Payette turns from south to north here before heading west toward Black Canyon Reservoir, giving Horseshoe Bend its name.
evidence.quote: It is named for its location at the horseshoe-shaped U-turn of the Payette River, whose flow direction changes from south to north before heading west to the Black Canyon Reservoir.

evidence.claim: Prospectors first used the place as a staging area, waiting beside the river for snow to thaw at higher elevations after the Boise Basin gold discovery of 1862.
evidence.quote: The area was originally settled as a gold miners' staging area, as prospectors waited along the river for snows to thaw at the higher elevations.  Gold had been discovered in 1862 in the Boise Basin mountains to the east, near Idaho City.

evidence.claim: Called Warrinersville after a sawmill operator, the settlement became Horseshoe Bend in 1867. Ranching and logging followed the gold rush, and a railroad from Emmett to Long Valley was completed in 1913.
evidence.quote: The settlement became known as Warrinersville, after a local sawmill operator.  The name was changed to Horseshoe Bend in 1867, and after the gold rush quieted, the city became a prosperous ranching and logging community.

evidence.claim: a railroad from Emmett to Long Valley was completed in 1913
evidence.quote: The railroad, from Emmett up to Long Valley following the Payette River (its North Fork above Banks), was completed in 1913.

evidence.claim: The sawmill operated by Boise Cascade, the city’s primary employer, closed on September 30, 1998.
evidence.quote: In 1998 the city's primary employer, Boise Cascade, closed its sawmill on September 30.

evidence.claim: The Payette River makes a horseshoe-shaped turn before flowing west toward Black Canyon Reservoir.
evidence.quote: the horseshoe-shaped U-turn of the Payette River, whose flow direction changes from south to north before heading west to the Black Canyon Reservoir.

flags: Byway lengths conflict across tourism captures: 52.7 miles (2014), 53 (2021), 56.8 in 2026 specifications and 57 in its prose. The numbered highway has its own 54.126-mile length. Omitted a single byway distance and drive time rather than equating these extents.
Paved two-lane description comes from the 2014 tourism capture; newer cache does not update lane configuration.
Dropped the current claim that the Falk store site was the only Boise–Umatilla stage stop: an older tourism page asserts this without corroboration in the cache.

Omitted current claims about visible Goodale Trail ruts and winter food gathering. The ruts appear in 2014/2021 tourism captures without a location or newer condition check; food gathering is generalized without a named community or community source. Did not equate the named trail with Highway 52.
Omitted “large, merry man” as an unhelpful subjective characterization, despite its presence in the town cache.

Emmett cache contains suspect text about the butte name and conflicts with other pages on François Payette’s Fort Boise dates. Those passages were not reused. All current moment titles, coordinates and orchard motifs are retained.
